e0-l001-charge-current-water-analogy.prompt: A 1 A current flows in a 1 mm² copper wire, yet the conduction electrons drift at only about 0.07 mm/s. Why does a lamp at the far end of a 10 m cable light almost instantly?
options: The electrons near the switch hop to the lamp at close to light speed, and the slow drift figure only applies to a wire carrying alternating current
The lamp filament holds a store of charge that is released first, and the supply electrons arrive later to replenish it as they drift along
Every part of the wire is already full of mobile electrons, and the field that pushes them spreads at near light speed, so all start moving together
The drift speed quoted is an average over a very long time, while individual electrons really run the cable length in a fraction of a second
e0-l001-charge-current-water-analogy.explanation: Drift is slow because carriers are dense (about 10²⁸ per m³) and collide constantly. The signal is the electric field set up along the wire, which propagates at a large fraction of c and moves the carriers everywhere at once.

e0-l001-charge-current-water-analogy.prompt: Which statement marks a place where the water-pipe analogy misleads?
options: Cut a wire and no steady current flows, since charge cannot spill into air the way water spills out of a cut pipe
Voltage corresponds to the flow rate of the water, so a larger voltage always means more charge passing per second in any wire
In a real circuit charge piles up in the thinner part of the wire, just as water slows and accumulates in a narrow pipe section
A longer, thinner wire has a lower resistance, because water flows more easily when a pipe is longer and narrower
e0-l001-charge-current-water-analogy.explanation: Voltage maps to pressure difference and current to flow rate; resistance rises with length and falls with area. Steady current needs a closed conducting loop, and charge does not pile up along a wire (net charge stays near zero).

e0-l001-charge-current-water-analogy.prompt: An electrolysis cell passes a steady 0.250 A for 2.00 h. How many moles of electrons are transferred? (Use F = 96485 C/mol; give the answer in mol.)
e0-l001-charge-current-water-analogy.explanation: Charge Q = It = 0.250 A × 7200 s = 1800 C, and n = Q/F = 1800/96485 = 0.0187 mol of electrons. For a 2-electron process that would deposit about half this many moles of metal.

e0-l001-charge-current-water-analogy.prompt: In your own words: why does a lamp light at once even though the electrons drift at millimetres per second, and in which direction does the conventional current point when electrons are the carriers?
e0-l001-charge-current-water-analogy.rubric: Full credit: (1) the wire is already full of mobile charge and the driving field spreads at near light speed, so carriers everywhere start together; (2) drift speed is small because of the huge carrier density (I = nqAv_d); (3) conventional current points opposite to the electron motion (the way positive charge would move).
e0-l001-charge-current-water-analogy.modelAnswer: The wire is already full of mobile electrons. Closing the switch sets up an electric field along the wire almost at light speed, and every electron feels it and starts drifting together, so the energy transfer is immediate. Because there are so many carriers, even a slow drift (I = nqAv_d) gives a large current. Conventional current is defined as the way positive charge would move, so with electrons carrying the current it points opposite to their motion.

e0-l002-voltage-energy-power.prompt: A 9 V battery and a 1.5 V cell each send one coulomb of charge through a lamp. Which statement is correct?
options: The 9 V battery stores nine times as much charge, so it delivers nine times the current through any lamp attached to it
Voltage is the amount of charge stored on the battery terminals, so the 9 V battery holds a larger charge than the AA cell does
Each coulomb gains the same energy from both, and the voltage only sets how fast the coulombs travel round the circuit
The 9 V battery gives each coulomb 9 J and the 1.5 V cell gives 1.5 J, so voltage is energy per unit charge
e0-l002-voltage-energy-power.explanation: 1 V = 1 J/C: the voltage is the energy given to each coulomb that passes. It does not by itself fix the current (that depends on the load) or the total charge stored (that is capacity, in A h).

e0-l002-voltage-energy-power.prompt: A 12 V car battery is being charged: 2 A flows into its positive terminal. What is the battery's power?
options: −24 W produced: a battery always supplies power to the circuit, whichever direction the current flows through it
+24 W absorbed: current enters the + terminal, so the charger delivers energy that is stored chemically
+24 W delivered by the battery to the charger, because the larger of the two voltages is the one supplying energy
0 W net: the current in and the chemical current out cancel, so no energy is exchanged while the battery is being charged
e0-l002-voltage-energy-power.explanation: With the passive sign convention, current entering the + terminal means the device absorbs P = IV = +24 W. The same battery supplies power when current leaves its + terminal. Charging stores this energy as chemical free energy.

e0-l002-voltage-energy-power.prompt: An AA cell is rated 2500 mAh at 1.5 V. How much energy is that? (Give the answer in kJ.)
e0-l002-voltage-energy-power.explanation: 2.5 A h × 3600 s/h = 9000 C, and 9000 C × 1.5 J/C = 13500 J = 13.5 kJ. Note that mAh counts charge, so the voltage must be included to get energy.

e0-l002-voltage-energy-power.prompt: A Daniell cell has E = 1.10 V. Explain in your own words what that number means in terms of energy per charge, and how it connects to ΔG = −nFE.
e0-l002-voltage-energy-power.rubric: Full credit: (1) 1.10 V means 1.10 J of electrical work per coulomb passed through the external circuit; (2) each mole of reaction moves n moles of electrons, i.e. nF coulombs, so the maximum work per mole is nFE = -ΔG; (3) notes it is a difference between the two electrodes.
e0-l002-voltage-energy-power.modelAnswer: A potential difference of 1.10 V means each coulomb that flows through the external circuit gains 1.10 J. A mole of reaction moves nF coulombs (n moles of electrons times 96485 C/mol), so the maximum electrical work per mole is nFE, which equals −ΔG for a reversible cell. For the 2-electron Daniell cell that is 2 × 96485 × 1.10 ≈ 212 kJ/mol. The voltage is always a difference between the two electrodes.

e0-l003-resistance-ohms-law-resistivity.prompt: A student plots current against voltage for a filament lamp and finds a curve that flattens at high voltage. What does that say about Ohm's law?
options: Ohm's law is violated, which proves that V = IR is false for any device that carries a high current in a metal
The ratio V/I is still defined at each point, but the lamp is non-ohmic because its resistance changes as it heats
The lamp is ohmic, because V = IR holds at every point and a curved plot only means the meter is out of calibration
The lamp's resistance falls with voltage because the filament gets hotter, and heat always makes the metal conduct better
e0-l003-resistance-ohms-law-resistivity.explanation: Ohm's law is the empirical statement that R = V/I is constant for a given conductor. A tungsten filament heats up, its resistance rises, and the I–V curve bends; V/I is still a valid number at each point.

e0-l003-resistance-ohms-law-resistivity.prompt: Heating a copper wire raises its resistance, but heating an NTC thermistor (a semiconductor) lowers its resistance. What is the main reason?
options: In the metal, heat adds carriers and in the semiconductor it removes them, since carriers are bound more tightly when it is warmer
Metals expand on heating so the wire gets longer and thinner; semiconductors contract and become shorter and fatter
The sign is a matter of how each material is doped, and the underlying carrier number and scattering do not change with temperature
In a metal, heating raises scattering; in a semiconductor, heating frees many more carriers, which outweighs the extra scattering
e0-l003-resistance-ohms-law-resistivity.explanation: In a metal the carrier density is fixed, so higher temperature only increases scattering and therefore resistance. In a semiconductor (or electrolyte) heating increases the number of mobile carriers dramatically, which outweighs the scattering.

e0-l003-resistance-ohms-law-resistivity.prompt: What is the resistance of a copper wire 2.0 m long and 0.50 mm in diameter? Use ρ = 1.68×10⁻⁸ Ω·m; give the answer in ohms.
e0-l003-resistance-ohms-law-resistivity.explanation: A = π(0.25 mm)² = 0.1963 mm² = 1.9635e-07 m², so R = ρL/A = 1.68×10⁻⁸ × 2.0 / 1.9635e-07 = 0.171 Ω. Doubling the diameter would cut it by a factor of four.

e0-l003-resistance-ohms-law-resistivity.prompt: Explain the difference between 'R = V/I' and 'Ohm's law', and give one device for which Ohm's law fails.
e0-l003-resistance-ohms-law-resistivity.rubric: Full credit: (1) R = V/I defines the resistance at an operating point for any device; (2) Ohm's law is the empirical statement that this ratio is constant over a range of V (and T); (3) gives a valid non-ohmic example (diode, lamp filament, thermistor, electrochemical cell) with a reason.
e0-l003-resistance-ohms-law-resistivity.modelAnswer: R = V/I is just a definition of the resistance at one operating point and can be computed for any device. Ohm's law is the experimental fact that for some materials, such as metal wires and resistors at constant temperature, this ratio does not depend on V or I, so the I–V plot is a straight line through the origin. A diode fails it: current rises exponentially with voltage and is almost zero below about 0.6 V.

e0-l004-resistor-codes-schematics.prompt: In a schematic, two wires cross at a point and there is no dot at the intersection. What does this mean?
options: They pass over each other without touching; only a dot (or a T-junction) shows that wires are connected
They are connected, since any two wires that cross on a drawing are joined at that point to form a single node
They are connected only if the two wires carry the same voltage, and otherwise they are treated as separate nodes
They are connected through a small stray capacitance, so DC signals stay separate but AC signals can pass between them
e0-l004-resistor-codes-schematics.explanation: In a schematic every node is a set of wires joined by dots or T-junctions. A bare crossing is only a drawing convenience, so the two wires can sit at different voltages.

e0-l004-resistor-codes-schematics.prompt: A 1 kΩ, ¼ W resistor is connected across a 20 V supply. What should you expect?
options: It carries 20 mA, which is a small current, so the resistor stays cool whatever its rated power is
It dissipates 0.02 W, which is far below the rating, since power is just the current times the resistance
It must dissipate 0.4 W, more than its rating, so it will overheat and may burn out
It dissipates 0.4 W, but ratings only apply to AC supplies, so on a steady DC supply it is safe
e0-l004-resistor-codes-schematics.explanation: P = V²/R = 400/1000 = 0.4 W, which exceeds 0.25 W. The rating limits power (heat) for AC and DC alike; the current alone says nothing about heating until you multiply by the voltage across the resistor.

e0-l004-resistor-codes-schematics.prompt: A resistor is banded green–blue–orange–gold (5, 6, ×10³, ±5%). What is the largest value it can have within tolerance? (Give the answer in kΩ.)
e0-l004-resistor-codes-schematics.explanation: The nominal value is 56 × 10³ Ω = 56 kΩ. With ±5% the top of the range is 56 × 1.05 = 58.8 kΩ, and the bottom is 53.2 kΩ. Gold means ±5%, not a digit.

e0-l004-resistor-codes-schematics.prompt: In your own words, how do you read a schematic as a set of nodes, and how would you use that to say what voltage is across a given resistor?
e0-l004-resistor-codes-schematics.rubric: Full credit: (1) every wire (joined by dots/T-junctions) is one node, one voltage; (2) pick a ground/reference node as 0 V; (3) the voltage across a component is the difference between the voltages of the nodes at its two ends.
e0-l004-resistor-codes-schematics.modelAnswer: Each connected set of wires is a single node, with one voltage everywhere on it. I pick a reference node (the ground symbol) as 0 V, label the other nodes, and the voltage across any component is just the difference between the voltages at its two end nodes. So to find the drop across a resistor I find its two end nodes and subtract.

e0-l005-series-parallel-resistors.prompt: Two 100 Ω resistors are in parallel. A third resistor is now added in parallel with them. The equivalent resistance of the group:
options: increases, because more resistor material is now placed between the two terminals of the source
stays at 50 Ω, because adding a branch to a parallel pair does not alter the voltage across the pair
increases only if the new resistor is larger than 100 Ω, and otherwise the group stays the same
decreases, because each new branch is an extra path for the current, so conductance increases
e0-l005-series-parallel-resistors.explanation: Parallel branches add conductance (G = 1/R), so adding any branch, even a huge resistor, lowers the total resistance slightly. Total resistance of a parallel group is always less than its smallest member.

e0-l005-series-parallel-resistors.prompt: Why are the lamps and appliances in a home wired in parallel rather than in series?
options: Parallel wiring makes the total resistance larger, which keeps the current drawn from the supply small and safe for the household wiring
Each gets the full mains voltage and works independently, while the total current is the sum of the branch currents
In series each appliance would get the full voltage, but all would draw the same current regardless of its rating
Parallel wiring ensures that the same current flows through every appliance, so that they all heat up equally
e0-l005-series-parallel-resistors.explanation: Parallel branches share the same voltage and each draws its own current. In series, the current is common and the voltage is split, so one failed lamp breaks the whole loop.

e0-l005-series-parallel-resistors.prompt: A 100 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 200 Ω and 300 Ω. What is the equivalent resistance? (Give the answer in ohms.)
e0-l005-series-parallel-resistors.explanation: 200 ‖ 300 = 200×300/500 = 120 Ω. In series with 100 Ω this gives 220 Ω.

e0-l005-series-parallel-resistors.prompt: Explain why the equivalent resistance of parallel resistors is always smaller than the smallest one, and say how you could check a reduced network.
e0-l005-series-parallel-resistors.rubric: Full credit: (1) each branch adds an extra path, i.e. adds conductance, so total conductance exceeds that of any single branch; (2) check by power conservation or by recomputing the source current from the equivalent resistance and comparing the sum of branch currents.
e0-l005-series-parallel-resistors.modelAnswer: Parallel resistors share the same voltage, and each branch carries its own current, so the total current is the sum. That means the conductances add, and the total conductance is larger than any one branch's, which means the total resistance is smaller than the smallest. To check a reduced network I compare the power from the source with the sum of I²R in all the original resistors, or compare the source current with the sum of branch currents.

e0-l006-voltage-current-dividers.prompt: A divider of two 10 kΩ resistors from a 10 V source gives 5.0 V. A 10 kΩ load is connected across the lower resistor. The output becomes about:
options: 5.0 V, because the output is set by the resistor ratio alone and a load connected afterwards cannot influence it
6.7 V, because the extra path draws more current, which raises the voltage across the lower resistor
3.3 V, because the load in parallel with the lower resistor leaves only 5 kΩ to share the 10 V with the upper one
2.5 V, because the load now forms a third equal share and the supply is divided equally among all three resistors in the chain
e0-l006-voltage-current-dividers.explanation: The lower leg becomes 10k ‖ 10k = 5 kΩ, so V_out = 10 × 5/(10+5) = 3.33 V. A divider is accurate only when the load is much larger than the resistor it sits across.

e0-l006-voltage-current-dividers.prompt: A designer wants the output of a divider to change by less than about 1% when a load is connected. What condition is the usual rule of thumb?
options: The load resistance should be about 100 times larger than the resistor it is connected across
The load resistance should be about 100 times smaller than that resistor, so that the load takes over the divider
The load resistance should be exactly equal to the sum of the two divider resistors for a matched result
The load resistance does not matter if both divider resistors are made large, since a divider is a passive part
e0-l006-voltage-current-dividers.explanation: The load shunts the lower resistor, lowering it by a fraction of order R_2/R_L. Keeping R_L ≥ 100 R_2 keeps that error near 1% or less (and the Thevenin view makes the same point).

e0-l006-voltage-current-dividers.prompt: A 3.0 mA current enters a node that splits into a 1.0 kΩ branch and a 2.0 kΩ branch in parallel. How much current flows through the 1.0 kΩ branch? (Give the answer in mA.)
e0-l006-voltage-current-dividers.explanation: I₁ = I × R₂/(R₁+R₂) = 3.0 × 2.0/3.0 = 2.0 mA. Check: the 2 kΩ branch gets 1.0 mA, and the voltage across both is 2 V.

e0-l006-voltage-current-dividers.prompt: Why does the current divider formula put the OTHER branch's resistance in the numerator? Mention one place a voltage divider is used in a real instrument.
e0-l006-voltage-current-dividers.rubric: Full credit: (1) current splits in proportion to conductance, so the smaller resistance takes the larger share; (2) hence I_1 = I·R_2/(R_1+R_2) for the branch with R_1; (3) a valid example such as a potentiometer, thermistor/photoresistor read-out or a scope probe.
e0-l006-voltage-current-dividers.modelAnswer: Current takes the easier path, and the branch currents are in proportion to the conductances. Branch 1 carries I × G₁/(G₁+G₂), which simplifies to I × R₂/(R₁+R₂), so the resistor of the other branch ends up on top. A potentiometer used as a volume or position control is a voltage divider, and so is a thermistor in series with a fixed resistor feeding an ADC.

e0-l007-kirchhoff-laws.prompt: What is the physical principle behind Kirchhoff's voltage law (the voltages around a closed loop sum to zero)?
options: Charge conservation: charge cannot build up in a loop, so the voltage gained must exactly equal the charge lost
Ohm's law: since V = IR for every element, the voltages around any loop must sum to zero, however the elements are connected
Energy conservation: a charge that returns to its starting point has no net energy change, so the rises equal the drops
The current is the same everywhere in a loop, so each element must drop the same share of the voltage
e0-l007-kirchhoff-laws.explanation: KVL says the potential is a single-valued function: going round a loop returns to the same potential. That is energy conservation. KCL is the charge-conservation law, applied at nodes.

e0-l007-kirchhoff-laws.prompt: After solving a circuit, you find the sources supply 12 W in total while the resistors absorb 11 W. What should you conclude?
options: There is an error somewhere, because in steady state supplied power must equal absorbed power
The solution is fine, since a little power is always lost in the wires and connections in any circuit
The missing 1 W is stored in the resistors, which warm up until they reach thermal equilibrium
Only KCL and KVL must be satisfied, and power balance is a separate result that need not hold exactly
e0-l007-kirchhoff-laws.explanation: Power balance is a consequence of KCL and KVL together (Tellegen's theorem). In an ideal-component model with no storage, the sum of supplied power equals the sum absorbed, so a mismatch signals an algebra or sign error.

e0-l007-kirchhoff-laws.prompt: A 12 V battery drives a series loop of 100 Ω, 220 Ω and 330 Ω. What is the voltage across the 330 Ω resistor? (Give the answer in volts.)
e0-l007-kirchhoff-laws.explanation: Series loop: I = 12/(100+220+330) = 18.46 mA. Then V = IR = 18.46 mA × 330 Ω = 6.09 V. The three drops sum to 12 V, as KVL requires.

e0-l007-kirchhoff-laws.prompt: In your own words, state KCL and KVL, name the conservation law behind each, and say why consistent sign conventions matter when you apply them.
e0-l007-kirchhoff-laws.rubric: Full credit: (1) KCL: currents into a node sum to zero (charge conservation); (2) KVL: voltages around a loop sum to zero (energy conservation); (3) the signs/orientations must be consistent, otherwise equations contradict and the answer may come out with wrong sign or magnitude.
e0-l007-kirchhoff-laws.modelAnswer: KCL says the current flowing into any node equals the current flowing out, because charge is conserved and a node cannot store charge. KVL says the voltage changes around any closed loop sum to zero, because energy is conserved and potential is single-valued. Both need a consistent choice of current directions and voltage polarities; a flipped sign in one term makes the equations disagree and gives the wrong answer.

e0-l008-nodal-analysis-linear-systems.prompt: Why does nodal analysis begin by choosing one node as the reference (ground)?
options: The ground node is the only one whose voltage is physically real, so every other voltage is measured against the earth itself
Kirchhoff's current law cannot be applied at a node that is connected to the negative terminal of a source
A reference node reduces the number of resistors in the problem by removing those connected to it
Only differences in voltage matter, so one node is set to 0 V and its own KCL equation is redundant
e0-l008-nodal-analysis-linear-systems.explanation: Adding a constant to every node voltage changes no current, so absolute voltages are not determined. Fixing one node at 0 V removes this freedom, and the N-th KCL equation is the sum of the others, hence redundant.

e0-l008-nodal-analysis-linear-systems.prompt: In the nodal equations G V = I for a resistor network, the matrix G is symmetric. What is the reason?
options: All resistors in a nodal problem must be equal, and equal conductances make the table of coefficients symmetric
The conductance joining node i and node j appears identically in both node equations, since a resistor treats both ends alike (reciprocity)
Kirchhoff's voltage law forces equal coefficients, and the current sources are chosen to keep the equations balanced
Symmetry only appears after row reduction, and the raw matrix of conductances has no particular pattern worth checking
e0-l008-nodal-analysis-linear-systems.explanation: The off-diagonal entry is −G_ij, the conductance between nodes i and j, and the same resistor gives the same −G_ji. The diagonal entry is the total conductance at the node. This is reciprocity, and it also gives a quick check on your matrix.

e0-l008-nodal-analysis-linear-systems.prompt: A 5 mA current source feeds node 1. A 1 kΩ resistor joins node 1 to ground, a 2 kΩ resistor joins node 1 to node 2, and a 2 kΩ resistor joins node 2 to ground. What is the voltage at node 2? (Give the answer in volts.)
e0-l008-nodal-analysis-linear-systems.explanation: KCL gives (1/1k + 1/2k)V₁ − (1/2k)V₂ = 5 mA and −(1/2k)V₁ + (1/2k + 1/2k)V₂ = 0. The second gives V₂ = V₁/2, then 1.25 mS × V₁ = 5 mA, so V₁ = 4.0 V and V₂ = 2.0 V.

e0-l008-nodal-analysis-linear-systems.prompt: Explain how nodal analysis turns a circuit into a linear system, and what would make the system fail to have a unique solution.
e0-l008-nodal-analysis-linear-systems.rubric: Full credit: (1) KCL at each non-reference node gives one linear equation in the node voltages, collected as G V = I; (2) solved by elimination/substitution (as in M0); (3) failure/singular if the network has a floating part with no path to the reference or equations are not independent.
e0-l008-nodal-analysis-linear-systems.modelAnswer: At each non-reference node I write KCL with currents expressed as conductance times voltage difference. That gives one linear equation per node, collected as G V = I, and I solve it by elimination or substitution like any system from algebra. The system is singular, with no unique solution, if some part of the circuit has no connection to the reference node (a floating section), because its voltages could all shift together.

e0-l009-mesh-analysis-superposition.prompt: A planar circuit has two meshes but four non-reference nodes and no current sources. Which method needs fewer equations?
options: Nodal analysis, because node voltages are easier to measure than loop currents, which are only mathematical objects
Mesh analysis, which needs two loop-current equations against four node-voltage equations
Both need four equations, because every element in the circuit must appear in at least one equation
Neither can be used until the circuit has been converted into a single series loop with one source
e0-l009-mesh-analysis-superposition.explanation: Choose the method with fewer unknowns: mesh currents number the independent loops, node voltages number the non-reference nodes. Both give the same answer, so counting first saves work.

e0-l009-mesh-analysis-superposition.prompt: A student finds the power in a resistor from each of two sources separately (with the other source turned off) and adds the two powers. Why is this wrong?
options: Power cannot be found from a source that is switched off, so each partial power calculation has no meaning
Superposition applies only to voltage sources, and the contribution of a current source must be found with a different method
The resistor absorbs power from only one source at a time, so the larger of the two partial powers is the right one
Power depends on the square of current or voltage, so partial powers do not add; add the currents first, then square
e0-l009-mesh-analysis-superposition.explanation: Superposition holds for linear relations such as V = IR, so currents and voltages add. Power P = I²R is quadratic: (I₁+I₂)² ≠ I₁² + I₂², because of the cross term 2I₁I₂.

e0-l009-mesh-analysis-superposition.prompt: A node is joined through 1 kΩ to a 10 V source, through another 1 kΩ to a 4 V source, and through a third 1 kΩ to ground. Use superposition to find the node voltage. (Give the answer in volts.)
e0-l009-mesh-analysis-superposition.explanation: 10 V alone: the other two resistors in parallel (0.5 kΩ) divide it, V = 10 × 0.5/1.5 = 3.333 V. 4 V alone: 1.333 V. The sum is 4.667 V.

e0-l009-mesh-analysis-superposition.prompt: Describe the superposition procedure for a circuit with two sources, including what each kind of source is replaced by, and why the method requires linearity.
e0-l009-mesh-analysis-superposition.rubric: Full credit: (1) turn on one source at a time; (2) replace an ideal voltage source by a short and a current source by an open circuit; (3) add the resulting currents/voltages; (4) works because the equations are linear (resistors, ideal sources), not for quadratic quantities such as power.
e0-l009-mesh-analysis-superposition.modelAnswer: I keep one source and turn the others off, replacing each ideal voltage source by a wire (short) and each current source by a break (open). I solve the simple circuit, repeat for each source, and add the results. It works because resistor circuits obey linear equations, so the response to a sum of sources is the sum of the responses; it fails for power, which is quadratic.

e0-l010-thevenin-norton.prompt: A battery reads 9.0 V with nothing connected but only 8.4 V when it powers a heavy load. How does the Thevenin model explain this?
options: The battery acts as a 9.0 V ideal source in series with a small internal resistance that drops part of the voltage under load
The chemical reaction produces less voltage when it is busy, so the ideal source itself falls to 8.4 V
The load carries too much power for the battery, and the missing voltage is stored in the wires and connectors until the load is removed
The battery behaves as an ideal current source, so its terminal voltage depends only on what the load happens to be
e0-l010-thevenin-norton.explanation: V_L = V_th R_L/(R_th + R_L), which is below V_th by the drop I·R_th across the internal resistance. The open-circuit voltage is V_th; heavier load (larger I) means a larger sag.

e0-l010-thevenin-norton.prompt: A Thevenin equivalent replaces a complicated network with one source and one resistor. What does it reproduce exactly?
options: Every voltage, current and power dissipation inside the original network, so the two circuits are the same in every way
The power dissipated inside the network, but not the voltage or current delivered to a load at its terminals
Voltage and current at the two terminals for any load, but not the power dissipated inside the original network (internal heating differs)
The behaviour at the terminals only for the particular load used in finding R_th, and for no other load
e0-l010-thevenin-norton.explanation: Equivalence is only external: any load connected to the terminals sees the same V and I. The internal heat is different (for example, an ideal Norton source with its parallel resistor dissipates power even with no load).

e0-l010-thevenin-norton.prompt: A 12 V source feeds a divider of 2 kΩ (top) and 4 kΩ (bottom). A 4 kΩ load is attached across the 4 kΩ resistor. Using a Thevenin equivalent of the divider, what is the load voltage? (Give the answer in volts.)
e0-l010-thevenin-norton.explanation: V_th = 12 × 4/6 = 8.0 V and R_th = 2k ‖ 4k = 1.333 kΩ. The load divides V_th: V_L = 8.0 × 4/(1.333+4) = 6.00 V.

e0-l010-thevenin-norton.prompt: How would you measure V_th and R_th of an unknown source in the lab, and what does each number tell you about the source?
e0-l010-thevenin-norton.rubric: Full credit: (1) V_th is the open-circuit voltage; (2) R_th from V_oc/I_sc (short circuit if safe), or by adding a load and finding the resistance at which the voltage falls to half; (3) interprets R_th as the source's internal resistance / how stiff it is.
e0-l010-thevenin-norton.modelAnswer: I measure the open-circuit voltage with a high-impedance meter, which gives V_th. For R_th I either measure the short-circuit current if that is safe (R_th = V_oc/I_sc), or connect a known load and use V_L = V_th R_L/(R_th+R_L), or find the load at which the voltage falls to half of V_th. R_th tells me how stiff the source is, that is, how much its voltage sags when current is drawn.

e0-l011-maximum-power-transfer.prompt: A source has V_th = 10 V and R_th = 50 Ω. It delivers maximum power to a load when R_L = 50 Ω. What is the efficiency (load power / total power) in that case?
options: 100%, because maximum power transfer by definition means that all the power produced reaches the load
25%, since only one quarter of the source voltage can ever be dropped across the load
Close to 90%, because the maximum power condition corresponds to the best possible efficiency of the source
50%, because the same current flows through the load and through the equal internal resistance
e0-l011-maximum-power-transfer.explanation: With R_L = R_th the current is the same through both and the two voltage drops are equal, so half the power is lost inside the source. Maximum power and maximum efficiency are different goals.

e0-l011-maximum-power-transfer.prompt: Why do a voltmeter input and a 230 kV power line deliberately NOT match their loads to the source resistance?
options: Matching only works for AC signals, and a power line or voltmeter works with direct current, so the rule does not apply
There the aim is accuracy or efficiency, not maximum power; matching would waste half the power or load the source
The load must be made much smaller than the source resistance so that the largest possible current is drawn
Matching works at low voltage only, because at high voltage the load resistance changes with temperature
e0-l011-maximum-power-transfer.explanation: A voltmeter should barely disturb the circuit (R_in ≫ R_th). A power line wants high efficiency, so the load resistance is much larger than the line resistance. Matching (50 Ω coax, RF) is chosen when delivering signal power or avoiding reflections matters.

e0-l011-maximum-power-transfer.prompt: A source with Thevenin resistance R_th drives a load R_L = 2 R_th. What fraction of the maximum available power does the load receive? (Give a number between 0 and 1.)
e0-l011-maximum-power-transfer.explanation: P_L = V²R_L/(R_th+R_L)² = V²(2R_th)/(3R_th)² = (2/9)V²/R_th, and P_max = V²/(4R_th) = 0.25 V²/R_th. The ratio is 0.889. The peak is broad: a factor-of-2 mismatch costs only 11%.

e0-l011-maximum-power-transfer.prompt: Show, using only algebra, why the load power is largest when R_L = R_th.
e0-l011-maximum-power-transfer.rubric: Full credit: (1) writes P_L = V_th^2 R_L/(R_th+R_L)^2; (2) uses (R_th+R_L)^2 = (R_th-R_L)^2 + 4R_thR_L ≥ 4R_thR_L, with equality only at R_L = R_th; (3) concludes P_L ≤ V_th^2/(4R_th).
e0-l011-maximum-power-transfer.modelAnswer: P_L = V_th² R_L/(R_th + R_L)². Expand the denominator as (R_th − R_L)² + 4R_th R_L. The first term is never negative, so the denominator is at least 4R_th R_L, which gives P_L ≤ V_th²/(4R_th). Equality holds only when R_th − R_L = 0, so the maximum is at R_L = R_th.

e0-l012-meters-loading-internal-resistan.prompt: How should an ideal ammeter be connected, and what resistance should it have?
options: In parallel with the component, with as little resistance as possible, so that the current flows easily into the meter
In series with the branch, with as much resistance as possible, so that the meter reads a clear voltage drop
In series with the branch, with as little resistance as possible, so that it does not change the current it measures
In parallel with the component, with as much resistance as possible, so that it draws no current from the circuit
e0-l012-meters-loading-internal-resistan.explanation: An ammeter must carry the branch current, so it goes in series and its resistance should be tiny (burden voltage I·R_meter is small). A voltmeter is the opposite: in parallel with a huge resistance.

e0-l012-meters-loading-internal-resistan.prompt: A pH glass electrode has a source resistance of about 100 MΩ. It is read by a meter with 10 MΩ input resistance. What happens?
options: The meter sees only about 9% of the electrode voltage, so an electrometer-grade input resistance is needed
Nothing important, since the meter has a lower resistance than the electrode and so passes the full signal
The meter sees 91% of the voltage, and a small calibration constant will correct the remaining 9%
The reading is correct only for a very short time, and the electrode's voltage then drifts as it is loaded by the meter
e0-l012-meters-loading-internal-resistan.explanation: The meter and the electrode's 100 MΩ form a divider: V_read = V×10/(100+10) = 9.1% of V. pH meters use input amplifiers with >10¹² Ω input resistance so this error is negligible.

e0-l012-meters-loading-internal-resistan.prompt: A 10 V source drives two 1 MΩ resistors in series. A multimeter with 10 MΩ input resistance is connected across the lower resistor. What does it read? (Give the answer in volts.)
e0-l012-meters-loading-internal-resistan.explanation: The lower leg becomes 1M ‖ 10M = 0.909 MΩ, so V = 10 × 0.909/(1 + 0.909) = 4.762 V instead of the true 5.000 V, an error of about 5%.

e0-l012-meters-loading-internal-resistan.prompt: Using the idea of a Thevenin equivalent, explain why connecting a voltmeter changes the voltage you are trying to measure, and what a four-wire (Kelvin) measurement of a small resistance fixes.
e0-l012-meters-loading-internal-resistan.rubric: Full credit: (1) circuit seen from the terminals = V_th + R_th; the meter's R_in forms a divider with R_th, so reading = V_th R_in/(R_th+R_in); good meter has R_in ≫ R_th; (2) four-wire uses separate current-carrying leads and voltage-sense leads, so lead and contact resistance do not appear in the voltage reading.
e0-l012-meters-loading-internal-resistan.modelAnswer: Seen from its terminals, the circuit is a source V_th with a series R_th. The meter's input resistance R_in forms a divider with R_th, so it reads V_th R_in/(R_th + R_in), which is low unless R_in is much larger than R_th. For a small resistance, a four-wire measurement drives the current through one pair of leads and senses the voltage with a separate pair that carries almost no current, so the lead and contact resistances produce no voltage error.

e0-l013-ground-shielding-safety.prompt: Two instruments on different wall outlets are linked by a shielded cable and the signal shows 50 Hz hum. What is the most likely cause?
options: The shielded cable is picking up the hum because shields collect interference from mains wiring and carry it along to the instrument
The two instruments are at exactly the same potential, and the hum is produced inside each one by its power transformer
A small voltage between the two ground points drives hum current through the cable shield, which adds to the signal (a ground loop)
The signal itself contains a 50 Hz component because all signals in an electronic circuit are modulated by the mains
e0-l013-ground-shielding-safety.explanation: Two different outlets give two slightly different ground potentials. The difference drives current round the loop formed by the grounds and the shield, producing a voltage along the cable. The usual fix is one ground point per signal path (or an isolation or differential input).

e0-l013-ground-shielding-safety.prompt: Which statement about electric shock is most accurate?
options: Harm depends on the current through the body, which is set by the voltage and the total body-plus-contact resistance
Only voltage matters, so any source under 50 V is harmless however low the skin resistance or large the supply is
Only the power rating of the supply matters, so a 1 kW source is always more dangerous than a 50 W one
Direct current is always safe, since it flows steadily in one direction, whereas alternating current is the only dangerous kind
e0-l013-ground-shielding-safety.explanation: Currents of about 1 mA are felt, 10–20 mA can prevent letting go, and ~100 mA through the chest can cause fibrillation. I = V/R_body, and wet skin can drop R_body from ~100 kΩ to ~1 kΩ, so context matters; DC at high voltage is also dangerous.

e0-l013-ground-shielding-safety.prompt: A person with wet hands (about 1.5 kΩ total resistance) touches a 120 V live conductor. What current flows through the body? (Give the answer in mA.)
e0-l013-ground-shielding-safety.explanation: I = V/R = 120/1500 = 80 mA. That is far above the ~10–20 mA let-go threshold and into the range where fibrillation is a risk, which is why dry hands, one-hand probing and GFCI protection matter.

e0-l013-ground-shielding-safety.prompt: In your own words, explain how 50/60 Hz noise gets into a signal cable and give two ways of reducing it. Why must you never remove the ground pin of an instrument's plug?
e0-l013-ground-shielding-safety.rubric: Full credit: (1) pickup by capacitive (electric field) and inductive (changing magnetic field) coupling and/or ground loops; (2) two valid remedies: shielding, twisted pair, coax, single-point grounding, differential input, shorter cable; (3) the ground pin carries fault current so that a short to the chassis trips the breaker rather than leaving the case live.
e0-l013-ground-shielding-safety.modelAnswer: Mains wiring has varying electric and magnetic fields that couple into the cable through stray capacitance and by induction, and differences between ground points drive currents through the shield. A shield, twisted pair or coax reduces this pickup, and connecting the shield to ground at one point avoids a ground loop. The ground pin gives fault current a low-resistance path so a short to the chassis blows the fuse or trips the breaker instead of leaving the case at mains voltage.

e0-l014-wheatstone-bridge.prompt: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when the detector reads zero. Why is a null measurement of this kind accurate?
options: The detector needs to be very accurate in volts to read the tiny leftover voltage at balance, so that is where the accuracy comes from
A balanced bridge forces the same current through all four resistors, so the unknown resistor equals the known one
At balance the bridge draws no current from the source, which makes the measurement independent of the resistor tolerances
At null the result depends only on resistor ratios, not on the source voltage or on the detector's calibration or gain
e0-l014-wheatstone-bridge.explanation: Balance requires R₁/R₂ = R₃/Rₓ, whatever the supply voltage is. The detector only has to tell zero from not zero, so its scale and linearity do not matter.

e0-l014-wheatstone-bridge.prompt: Why is a sensor resistance usually placed in a bridge instead of in a simple voltage divider?
options: The bridge makes ΔR itself larger, which increases the sensitivity of the sensing element to temperature or strain
The bridge cancels the large constant offset, so a tiny ΔR shows up near 0 V and can be amplified with high gain
The bridge supplies more power to the sensor, so that the output signal is larger than that of a divider
The bridge removes the need for a power supply, because the sensor resistance generates its own voltage
e0-l014-wheatstone-bridge.explanation: A divider output sits near V_s/2 and the small change rides on top of it; the bridge subtracts the matched reference arm, leaving only ≈ V_sΔR/(4R). The same trick makes conductivity, strain and thermal-conductivity measurements sensitive.

e0-l014-wheatstone-bridge.prompt: A strain gauge of R = 350 Ω in one arm of an otherwise balanced bridge changes by +0.35 Ω with V_s = 5.0 V. What is the bridge output? (Give the answer in mV.)
e0-l014-wheatstone-bridge.explanation: V_out ≈ V_s ΔR/(4R) = 5.0 × 0.35/1400 = 1.250 mV; the exact formula gives 1.249 mV. A 0.1% change in R produces only about a quarter of a millivolt per volt of excitation, so the signal is small.

e0-l014-wheatstone-bridge.prompt: Explain in your own words why the bridge balance condition is R₁/R₂ = R₃/Rₓ, and give one chemistry or instrument example of a bridge sensor (and why AC may be used).
e0-l014-wheatstone-bridge.rubric: Full credit: (1) at balance the two midpoints are at equal voltage, so the two dividers have equal ratios; (2) hence R_x/(R_x+R_3) = R_2/(R_1+R_2) leading to the stated ratio; (3) a valid example, e.g. conductivity cell with AC to avoid electrolysis/polarisation, thermal-conductivity detector, Pirani gauge, strain gauge, thermistor.
e0-l014-wheatstone-bridge.modelAnswer: Each side of the bridge is a voltage divider. If the two midpoints are at the same voltage the detector reads zero, which means the two divider ratios are equal, and rearranging gives R₁/R₂ = R₃/Rₓ. A conductivity cell is measured in a bridge with an AC supply so that the electrodes do not polarise or electrolyse the solution; a thermal-conductivity detector in a gas chromatograph is another bridge sensor.

e0-l015-capacitors.prompt: A capacitor stays connected to a battery while a dielectric with ε_r = 4 fills the gap between its plates. What happens?
options: C rises four-fold, but the stored energy falls to a quarter because the dielectric weakens the electric field
C rises four-fold, the battery supplies extra charge, and the stored energy ½CV² rises four-fold
C stays the same because it depends only on geometry, but the charge on the plates falls four-fold
C rises four-fold and the voltage across the plates also rises four-fold, so the stored energy rises sixteen-fold
e0-l015-capacitors.explanation: With V fixed by the battery, C → ε_r C means Q = CV rises ε_r-fold, and U = ½CV² rises ε_r-fold. The dielectric's induced dipoles cancel part of the field so the plates can hold more charge at the same voltage.

e0-l015-capacitors.prompt: A 10 µF capacitor is connected across a steady 5 V DC supply. After a long time the current through it is:
options: 5 A, since a capacitor of 10 µF passes a current equal to its voltage divided by the capacitance
Constant and non-zero, because electrons continue to flow through the dielectric as long as the voltage is applied
Zero only because the capacitor is full of charge, and it would carry current again if the voltage were doubled
essentially zero, since current flows only while the voltage across the capacitor is changing (I = CΔV/Δt)
e0-l015-capacitors.explanation: A capacitor current is proportional to the rate of change of voltage: with ΔV/Δt = 0 there is none. A larger steady voltage would just store more charge. Fast changes (high frequency) pass easily, which is why capacitors block DC but pass AC.

e0-l015-capacitors.prompt: A 100 µF capacitor is charged to 12 V. How much energy does it store? (Give the answer in mJ.)
Explain physically why capacitors in parallel add but capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel.
e0-l015-capacitors.rubric: Full credit: (1) parallel = plates side by side, effectively larger area, so C = εA/d increases and capacitances add; (2) series = effectively larger total plate separation (same charge on each, voltages add), so C is smaller than any single one and 1/C_total = Σ 1/C_i.
e0-l015-capacitors.modelAnswer: Capacitors in parallel behave like one capacitor with the plate areas added, and since C = εA/d the capacitances add. In series the same charge sits on each capacitor and the voltages add, which acts like a larger total plate separation, so the combination has a smaller capacitance and 1/C_total is the sum of the 1/C_i.

e0-l016-inductors.prompt: A coil carrying a steady current is disconnected abruptly with a switch. What do you expect, and why?
options: A large voltage spike across the switch, because V = LΔI/Δt is huge when the current is forced to change in a tiny time
Nothing unusual, since the stored energy is zero as soon as the battery is disconnected and no current can flow
A large current surge, because the coil resists any change in voltage and releases its stored charge at once
A smooth, slow decay in the voltage, because inductors cannot produce more voltage than the battery that charged them in the first place
e0-l016-inductors.explanation: An inductor resists changes in current. Forcing the current to change quickly (small Δt) makes V = LΔI/Δt large, enough to arc across a switch. A flyback diode gives the current a path to decay safely.

e0-l016-inductors.prompt: Which pairing correctly describes the two reactive components?
options: A capacitor resists changes in current; an inductor resists changes in voltage
A capacitor and an inductor both resist changes in current, but one stores energy and the other dissipates it
A capacitor resists changes in voltage; an inductor resists changes in current
A capacitor resists changes in voltage; an inductor resists steady currents of every kind, including DC
e0-l016-inductors.explanation: I = CΔV/Δt means a capacitor's voltage cannot jump (that would need infinite current); V = LΔI/Δt means an inductor's current cannot jump. At DC an ideal inductor is just a wire.

e0-l016-inductors.prompt: A solenoid has 500 turns, length 5.0 cm and radius 1.0 cm, with air inside. What is its inductance? (Use L = μ₀N²A/ℓ; give the answer in mH.)
e0-l016-inductors.explanation: A = π(0.010)² = 3.14×10⁻⁴ m², so L = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 500² × 3.14×10⁻⁴ / 0.050 = 1.97 mH. L grows as N², so doubling the turns quadruples it.

e0-l016-inductors.prompt: Explain why an inductor stores energy in its magnetic field and why opening a switch in series with a coil can produce a spark.
e0-l016-inductors.rubric: Full credit: (1) current builds a magnetic field and work done against the induced emf is stored as ½LI²; (2) the coil opposes changes in current, so interrupting it quickly induces a large emf V = LΔI/Δt; (3) this voltage can exceed the breakdown voltage of the gap and arc, dissipating the stored energy.
e0-l016-inductors.modelAnswer: While the current builds up, the changing magnetic flux induces a back emf, and the work done against it is stored in the field as ½LI². If the switch interrupts the current abruptly, the coil still tries to keep the current going and its induced voltage LΔI/Δt becomes very large. That can exceed the breakdown voltage of the switch gap, so a spark carries the stored energy away.

e0-l017-rc-rl-time-constant.prompt: Why does a capacitor charge through a resistor along an exponential curve and not at a steady rate?
options: The capacitor's resistance grows linearly as charge accumulates, which slows the charging in direct proportion to time
The source voltage itself decays while the capacitor charges, which makes each later step smaller than the last
The time constant lengthens as charging proceeds, because RC increases whenever more charge is stored on the plates
The current is set by the voltage still left across the resistor, so the rate of rise shrinks as the capacitor fills and the gap narrows
e0-l017-rc-rl-time-constant.explanation: I = (V_s − V_C)/R, so the rate of change of V_C is proportional to V_s − V_C, the 'distance left to go'. Rate proportional to what remains gives an exponential approach (the same law as first-order decay in kinetics).

e0-l017-rc-rl-time-constant.prompt: Both R and C of a charging circuit are doubled. How does the time constant change?
options: It doubles, since only the larger of the two components controls the speed of the whole charging process in the circuit
It grows four-fold: a larger R limits the current and a larger C needs more charge for the same voltage change
It stays the same, because the charge needed and the current available both rise together
It falls by half, because a bigger capacitor offers a larger area through which current can flow
e0-l017-rc-rl-time-constant.explanation: τ = RC, so doubling both gives 4×: a larger R reduces the current while a larger C needs twice the charge to reach the same voltage. Both effects slow the circuit.

e0-l017-rc-rl-time-constant.prompt: R = 10 kΩ and C = 1.0 µF. How long does it take the capacitor to charge to 99% of the supply voltage? (Use t = τ ln 100; give the answer in ms.)
e0-l017-rc-rl-time-constant.explanation: τ = RC = 10 ms. From 1 − e^(−t/τ) = 0.99, e^(−t/τ) = 0.01 and t = τ ln 100 = 46.1 ms, about 4.6τ.

e0-l017-rc-rl-time-constant.prompt: Define the time constant for an RC and an RL circuit, and name one laboratory analogue of the same exponential behaviour (NMR, electrochemistry or an ADC).
e0-l017-rc-rl-time-constant.rubric: Full credit: (1) τ_RC = RC and τ_RL = L/R, the time to reach ~63% of the final change; (2) the shape is exponential because the rate is proportional to the remaining difference; (3) gives a valid analogue: T1 relaxation, double-layer charging in cyclic voltammetry, or settling of an ADC input.
e0-l017-rc-rl-time-constant.modelAnswer: The time constant is τ = RC for an RC circuit and τ = L/R for an RL circuit; after one τ the circuit has covered about 63% of its change and after five τ about 99%. The same exponential law appears in NMR T1 relaxation (the magnetisation approaches equilibrium at a rate proportional to the distance left), in the charging of the electrode double layer through the solution resistance, and in the settling of an RC filter before an ADC.

e0-l018-sinusoids-rms-phase.prompt: A 5 V rms sine wave has an average value of zero over a cycle. Why does it still heat a resistor?
options: Only the positive half-cycles drive current through the resistor, while the negative half-cycles are blocked by it
The average voltage is zero, but the resistor stores the heat from the positive halves until the negative halves arrive, which then cancel it out
Power goes as v²/R, which is never negative, so the heating averages to a positive value while the voltage averages to zero
The resistor responds to the peak voltage only, so the heating is set by V_p and not by an average
e0-l018-sinusoids-rms-phase.explanation: Heating is quadratic in voltage: P = v²/R ≥ 0. The mean of v² is V_p²/2, so V_rms = V_p/√2 is the DC voltage that would give the same average heating.

e0-l018-sinusoids-rms-phase.prompt: A sine wave of fixed peak value is made to oscillate twice as fast. Which of its properties changes?
options: The period halves and the frequency doubles, while the amplitude and the RMS value stay as they were
The RMS value doubles with the frequency, since faster oscillations carry more energy per second
The period doubles, because the wave now needs more time to complete its cycle between zero crossings
The peak value doubles with the frequency, because the voltage has less time to reach its maximum
e0-l018-sinusoids-rms-phase.explanation: f = 1/T, so doubling f halves T; amplitude and RMS are set by the peak value alone. Frequency matters later through the reactances ωL and 1/(ωC).

e0-l018-sinusoids-rms-phase.prompt: A wall outlet supplies 120 V rms sinusoidal mains. What is its peak-to-peak voltage? (Give the answer in volts.)
e0-l018-sinusoids-rms-phase.explanation: V_p = 120√2 = 169.7 V, so the peak-to-peak value is 2V_p = 339 V. This is why insulation and capacitor voltage ratings must be chosen for the peak, not the rms value.

e0-l018-sinusoids-rms-phase.prompt: On a two-channel scope, channel B's peak occurs 0.6 ms after channel A's, and both signals are at 400 Hz. Explain how to find the phase difference and what 'B lags A' means.
e0-l018-sinusoids-rms-phase.rubric: Full credit: (1) period T = 1/f = 2.5 ms; (2) phase = 360° × Δt/T = 86.4° (about 86°); (3) 'lags' means B reaches each feature later than A, i.e. B is delayed relative to A.
e0-l018-sinusoids-rms-phase.modelAnswer: The period is 1/400 Hz = 2.5 ms. A delay of 0.6 ms is a fraction 0.6/2.5 = 0.24 of a cycle, so the phase difference is 360° × 0.24 = 86.4°, close to a quarter cycle. 'B lags A' means each peak of B happens after the matching peak of A.

e0-l019-phasors-complex-numbers.prompt: What does a phasor keep, and what does it leave out, when it represents a sinusoid in a linear circuit?
options: It keeps frequency and amplitude, and leaves out the phase, since phase is only needed for non-linear circuits
It keeps phase and frequency, and leaves out the amplitude, which is fixed by the source and never changes
It keeps amplitude and phase, and leaves out the frequency, which is common to every signal in the circuit
It keeps only the instantaneous value at t = 0, which is enough to rebuild the entire waveform
e0-l019-phasors-complex-numbers.explanation: In a linear circuit driven at one frequency, every voltage and current oscillates at that frequency, so only amplitude and phase differ from place to place. The phasor stores those two numbers as one complex number.

e0-l019-phasors-complex-numbers.prompt: Multiplying a phasor by j has what effect?
options: It rotates the phasor by +90° without changing its length, which turns a cosine into a negative sine
It doubles the phasor's length and leaves the angle unchanged, which doubles the amplitude of the wave
It rotates the phasor by 180°, which reverses the sign of the signal while keeping its amplitude
It converts the phasor into a real number, which is why j never appears in measured quantities
e0-l019-phasors-complex-numbers.explanation: j = e^{jπ/2}, so multiplying by j adds 90° to the angle and leaves the magnitude alone. In a capacitor or inductor, I ∝ jωCV or V ∝ jωLI is exactly this 90° shift (calculus later shows it comes from a derivative).

e0-l019-phasors-complex-numbers.prompt: Two voltages at the same frequency are v₁ = 6 V sin(ωt) and v₂ = 8 V sin(ωt + 90°). What is the amplitude of their sum? (Give the answer in volts.)
e0-l019-phasors-complex-numbers.explanation: As phasors: 6 + j8, whose magnitude is √(36+64) = 10 V. Adding amplitudes (6 + 8 = 14 V) would be wrong: the two waves peak at different times.

e0-l019-phasors-complex-numbers.prompt: Why can't you add the amplitudes of two sinusoids of the same frequency when they are out of phase, and how does the phasor method fix this?
e0-l019-phasors-complex-numbers.rubric: Full credit: (1) peaks occur at different times, so the sum is smaller than the sum of amplitudes (unless in phase); (2) represent each as a complex number (amplitude and angle), add as complex numbers (vector addition); (3) magnitude of the sum is the amplitude, angle is the phase.
e0-l019-phasors-complex-numbers.modelAnswer: The two waves reach their maxima at different times, so the sum never reaches the sum of the two amplitudes unless they are in phase. With phasors each wave becomes a complex number with the wave's amplitude and phase. I add them like vectors, and the magnitude and angle of the result are the amplitude and phase of the summed wave.

e0-l020-impedance-reactance.prompt: For an ideal capacitor driven by a sine wave, how are the current and voltage related?
options: The current lags the voltage by 90°: it is largest when the voltage is at its peak, because the capacitor is then fully charged
The current and voltage are in phase, because a capacitor has a fixed ratio of voltage to current like a resistor
The current leads the voltage by 180°, since the capacitor delivers current in the direction that opposes the voltage
The current leads the voltage by 90°: it is largest when the voltage is changing fastest, which is at the zero crossings
e0-l020-impedance-reactance.explanation: I = CΔV/Δt: current is biggest where V changes fastest (zero crossings) and zero at the peaks, so it leads by 90°. For an inductor the roles reverse and the current lags.

e0-l020-impedance-reactance.prompt: As the frequency of a sine source is raised, what happens to the magnitudes of the impedances of a capacitor and an inductor?
options: The capacitor's impedance rises as ωC and the inductor's falls as 1/ωL, since both respond to faster change
The capacitor's impedance falls as 1/ωC and the inductor's rises as ωL
Both rise in proportion to frequency, because faster oscillations make any storage element harder to drive
Both are unchanged, because reactance is a property of the component and the frequency only changes the phase
e0-l020-impedance-reactance.explanation: |Z_C| = 1/(ωC) goes to zero at high frequency (a short) and infinity at DC (open); |Z_L| = ωL goes to zero at DC (a wire) and rises at high frequency. This is the basis of filters.

e0-l020-impedance-reactance.prompt: A 1.0 kΩ resistor is in series with a 0.10 µF capacitor driven at 1.0 kHz. What is the magnitude of the total impedance? (Give the answer in ohms.)
e0-l020-impedance-reactance.explanation: X_C = 1/(2π f C) = 1/(2π × 1000 × 10⁻⁷) = 1592 Ω. Then |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) = √(1000² + 1592²) = 1880 Ω. The reactance adds at right angles to R, not directly.

e0-l020-impedance-reactance.prompt: Why does an ideal capacitor or inductor dissipate no power on average, even though current flows through it?
e0-l020-impedance-reactance.rubric: Full credit: (1) voltage and current are 90° apart, so the instantaneous power v·i alternates positive and negative with zero average; (2) the component stores energy in its field in one quarter-cycle and returns it in the next; (3) only the resistive part dissipates energy as heat.
e0-l020-impedance-reactance.modelAnswer: Current and voltage are 90° out of phase in a capacitor or inductor, so the instantaneous power vi is positive for a quarter cycle (energy flows into the stored electric or magnetic field) and negative for the next (the energy is returned to the source). The average is zero. Only resistance turns energy into heat.

e0-l021-filters-frequency-dividers.prompt: An RC low-pass filter has a cut-off frequency of 1 kHz. What does it do to a 10 kHz component of the signal?
options: It passes it unchanged, since a low-pass filter only affects the phase of components that lie above its cut-off frequency
It cuts it to about 10% of its amplitude (−20 dB), since the roll-off is 20 dB per decade above the cut-off
It removes it completely, since everything above the cut-off frequency is blocked by a low-pass filter
It cuts it to about 71% of its amplitude, since this is the gain that the filter has at every frequency
e0-l021-filters-frequency-dividers.explanation: |H| = 1/√(1+(f/f_c)²) = 1/√101 = 0.100, or −20 dB. The filter is a divider whose lower leg, the capacitor, has smaller impedance at higher frequency. At f_c exactly the gain is 0.707 (−3 dB).

e0-l021-filters-frequency-dividers.prompt: A chemist lowers the cut-off of an RC filter on a detector to reduce noise. What is the trade-off?
options: More noise bandwidth, but a faster response, so the peaks are sharper and the baseline is noisier than before for a given signal
Less noise and no loss of signal, because a filter acts only on frequencies that carry noise and never on a peak
The same noise, but the peaks arrive earlier, since the filter advances the signal by one time constant
Less noise bandwidth, but a slower response (rise time ≈ 0.35/f_c), so sharp, narrow peaks are smeared and reduced
e0-l021-filters-frequency-dividers.explanation: Noise power scales with bandwidth, so a smaller f_c helps; but the time constant τ = RC = 1/(2πf_c) grows, so fast features are rounded off. Choose f_c comfortably above the signal's own bandwidth.

e0-l021-filters-frequency-dividers.prompt: What is the cut-off frequency of an RC low-pass filter with R = 4.7 kΩ and C = 0.22 µF? (Give the answer in Hz.)
In your own words, explain why an RC filter is just a voltage divider, and why that makes it low-pass (or high-pass) depending on which part the output is taken across.
e0-l021-filters-frequency-dividers.rubric: Full credit: (1) the capacitor's impedance 1/(ωC) changes with frequency, so the divider ratio depends on frequency; (2) output across C: at low f, Z_C is large so most voltage appears (passes), at high f Z_C is small (attenuated) = low-pass; (3) output across R gives the opposite, high-pass.
e0-l021-filters-frequency-dividers.modelAnswer: The filter is two impedances in series with the output taken across one of them, which is the divider formula. The capacitor's impedance 1/(ωC) is large at low frequency and small at high frequency, so the divider ratio changes with frequency. With the output across the capacitor, low frequencies pass and high ones are shorted, a low-pass filter; swapping the roles of R and C, the output across R passes high frequencies, a high-pass filter.

e0-l022-rlc-resonance.prompt: What is true of a series RLC circuit at its resonant frequency?
options: The reactances cancel, so the impedance is just R and the current peaks in phase with the voltage; only the resistor limits that peak
The inductive and capacitive reactances add to their maximum, so the impedance is largest and the current is smallest
The resistance falls to zero because the energy is exchanged without loss, and the current rises without limit
The current and voltage are 90° out of phase, because the inductor and capacitor both resist the flow of AC
e0-l022-rlc-resonance.explanation: At ω₀ the reactances ωL and 1/(ωC) are equal and opposite, leaving |Z| = R. The current is largest and in phase with the source; the resistor limits it, so it stays finite.

e0-l022-rlc-resonance.prompt: An NMR probe circuit is built to have a higher Q. What does that change?
options: The resonance peak becomes wider and lower, so the circuit responds equally to every frequency near the Larmor frequency
The resonant frequency rises in proportion to Q, so the capacitor must be retuned to bring it back to the same value
The peak becomes narrower and taller, so it is more selective, but it rings longer after a pulse
The energy stored in the circuit falls, because a higher Q means that more of it is dissipated in each cycle
e0-l022-rlc-resonance.explanation: Q = ω₀L/R = f₀/Δf: lower loss R gives a narrower bandwidth, and energy decays over about Q/π cycles. High Q improves sensitivity but gives a longer ring-down (dead time) after the RF pulse.

e0-l022-rlc-resonance.prompt: An LC circuit has L = 10 µH and C = 100 pF. What is its resonant frequency? (Give the answer in MHz.)
e0-l022-rlc-resonance.explanation: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(10⁻⁵ × 10⁻¹⁰)) = 5.03 MHz. Tuning such a circuit to a Larmor frequency (e.g. several hundred MHz in a high-field NMR probe) is done with small variable capacitors.

e0-l022-rlc-resonance.prompt: Explain how an LC circuit oscillates, using the words 'electric field', 'magnetic field' and 'energy', and say how that resembles a mass on a spring.
e0-l022-rlc-resonance.rubric: Full credit: (1) energy is stored alternately in the capacitor's electric field and the inductor's magnetic field; (2) charge flows until the capacitor is empty, the inductor's current keeps it going and recharges the capacitor with opposite polarity; (3) analogy: capacitor = spring (potential energy), inductor = mass (kinetic/inertia), resistance = friction.
e0-l022-rlc-resonance.modelAnswer: The charged capacitor stores energy in its electric field. It discharges through the inductor, whose current builds a magnetic field that holds the energy; when the capacitor is empty, the inductor's current keeps flowing and recharges the capacitor with the opposite polarity. The energy slops back and forth just as a mass on a spring swaps potential and kinetic energy, with the inductor as the mass, the capacitor as the spring and resistance as friction.

e0-l023-diodes-leds-rectifiers.prompt: Why does an LED behave like a nearly fixed voltage drop (say 2 V), and why must a resistor be used in series with it?
options: The LED has a fixed resistance of about 2 Ω per volt, so the resistor is needed only to protect it from voltage spikes
The LED stores charge up to 2 V, and the resistor drains that charge so that the light output stays steady
The current is proportional to the voltage across it, and the resistor is needed to keep the colour constant
Current rises about tenfold per 60 mV (a Boltzmann factor), so tiny voltage changes mean huge current changes; the resistor sets it
e0-l023-diodes-leds-rectifiers.explanation: I = I_s(e^(V/V_T) − 1) is exponential (a Boltzmann factor): +60 mV gives ×10.3 in current. Over the useful range V barely moves, so it is the series resistor, R = (V_s − V_f)/I, that sets the current.

e0-l023-diodes-leds-rectifiers.prompt: A bridge rectifier feeds a smoothing capacitor. What happens to the ripple if the capacitance is increased?
options: The ripple rises, because a larger capacitor takes longer to charge and so follows the peaks of the waveform less closely
The ripple falls, since the capacitor discharges less between peaks (ΔV ≈ I/fC), but recharges in larger, shorter pulses
The ripple is unchanged, because it is set only by the mains frequency and the transformer voltage
The ripple falls and the diode current also falls, because the capacitor supplies charge continuously to the load
e0-l023-diodes-leds-rectifiers.explanation: Between peaks the capacitor supplies the load, losing ΔV ≈ IΔt/C = I/(fC) (f is 100/120 Hz for a full-wave rectifier). A bigger C lowers ripple but must recharge in a shorter conduction window, so the peak diode current rises.

e0-l023-diodes-leds-rectifiers.prompt: A red LED with a forward voltage of 2.0 V is to carry 10 mA from a 5.0 V supply. What series resistor is needed? (Give the answer in ohms.)
e0-l023-diodes-leds-rectifiers.explanation: R = (V_s − V_f)/I = (5.0 − 2.0)/0.010 = 300 Ω. The resistor dissipates 30 mW, well within a ¼ W part.

e0-l023-diodes-leds-rectifiers.prompt: Describe in words what happens inside a p–n junction when it is forward-biased, and why the current depends exponentially on voltage (mention a Boltzmann factor).
e0-l023-diodes-leds-rectifiers.rubric: Full credit: (1) forward bias reduces the potential barrier of the depletion region so carriers can cross; (2) the number of carriers with enough energy to cross the barrier is proportional to a Boltzmann factor e^(qV/kT); (3) so the current grows exponentially with V, and reverse bias gives only a small leakage current.
e0-l023-diodes-leds-rectifiers.modelAnswer: The depletion region creates a potential barrier that stops majority carriers crossing. Forward bias lowers the barrier by qV, and the number of carriers with enough thermal energy to get over it grows as a Boltzmann factor, e^(qV/kT), so the current rises exponentially with voltage. Under reverse bias the barrier gets higher and only a tiny leakage current flows.

e0-l024-transistors-switch-amplifier.prompt: When a bipolar transistor is used as a switch to turn on an LED, how should the base current be chosen?
options: Equal to the LED current, since the base current must carry the same charge as the collector in order to switch the LED on
As small as possible, since any base current heats the transistor and only the voltage at the base matters
Large enough that I_B exceeds I_C/β, so the transistor saturates like a closed switch, with a base resistor limiting it
Chosen so that the transistor stays in its linear region, so that the LED current follows the base current exactly
e0-l024-transistors-switch-amplifier.explanation: In the linear region I_C = βI_B. To use the device as a switch you overdrive the base (I_B ≥ I_C/β, usually several times) so that it saturates with only a few tenths of a volt across it.

e0-l024-transistors-switch-amplifier.prompt: In a common-emitter amplifier, why is the output an inverted copy of the input?
options: A rising input raises the collector current, which increases the drop across R_C, so the collector voltage falls
A rising input reduces the collector current, because the transistor opposes any change in its base voltage
The transistor subtracts the base voltage from the supply, so the output is the supply minus the input voltage
The output is inverted by the capacitor that couples the signal in, and the transistor itself has no part in it at all
e0-l024-transistors-switch-amplifier.explanation: I_C increases with the base voltage, so V_C = V_CC − I_C R_C decreases: gain A_v = −R_C/r_e is negative. The bias point keeps the transistor in its linear region so that signals of both polarities are amplified.

e0-l024-transistors-switch-amplifier.prompt: A transistor stage has I_E = 1.0 mA and R_C = 4.7 kΩ. Using r_e ≈ 25 mV/I_E, what is the magnitude of the small-signal voltage gain? (Give a number.)
e0-l024-transistors-switch-amplifier.explanation: r_e = 25 mV/1 mA = 25 Ω, so |A_v| = R_C/r_e = 4700/25 = 188. The gain is large but depends on temperature and I_E, which is why op-amps with feedback are preferred for precision.

e0-l024-transistors-switch-amplifier.prompt: Explain the transistor as a 'controlled valve': what controls what, and where the extra power in the output comes from.
e0-l024-transistors-switch-amplifier.rubric: Full credit: (1) a small base current (or gate voltage) controls a much larger collector (drain) current; (2) the output power comes from the power supply, not from the input; (3) the input only steers how much of the supply's current flows through the load.
e0-l024-transistors-switch-amplifier.modelAnswer: A small base current (or gate voltage) opens or closes the path for a much larger collector current, like a small force on a tap handle controlling a large water flow. The larger output power comes from the supply voltage, not from the input signal; the transistor just steers how much of that supply's current passes through the load.

e0-l025-opamp-golden-rules-inverting.prompt: Why can we assume the two inputs of an op-amp with negative feedback sit at (almost) the same voltage?
options: The two inputs are physically connected inside the op-amp, so they cannot be at different voltages in any circuit
The op-amp produces the same output for any input difference, so the voltage between the inputs does not matter
The output is finite, so V_+ − V_− = V_out/A is tiny for a huge A, and feedback adjusts V_out to keep it so, as negative feedback always does
Negative feedback sends equal currents into both inputs, so the voltages are bound to match
e0-l025-opamp-golden-rules-inverting.explanation: V_out = A(V_+ − V_−) with A ~ 10⁵ and |V_out| ≤ a few volts means the difference is microvolts. Feedback adjusts V_out so that this is true: the first golden rule. Without feedback, the same gain just saturates the output.

e0-l025-opamp-golden-rules-inverting.prompt: In the inverting amplifier the inverting input is called a 'virtual ground'. What does that mean?
options: Feedback holds it at about 0 V, but it is not connected to ground and almost no current flows into it
It is connected to ground through a very high resistance, which pulls the voltage at that input to zero
It is at 0 V because the output is always zero, so no voltage is dropped across the feedback resistor
It is a real ground, which is why the op-amp can supply any current that the input resistor asks for
e0-l025-opamp-golden-rules-inverting.explanation: Since V_+ = 0 and V_− ≈ V_+, the input node sits near 0 V. The input current V_in/R_in cannot enter the op-amp, so it flows through R_f: V_out = −V_in R_f/R_in.

e0-l025-opamp-golden-rules-inverting.prompt: An inverting amplifier has R_in = 10 kΩ and R_f = 47 kΩ. What is the output voltage for a +0.20 V input? (Give the answer in volts, with sign.)
e0-l025-opamp-golden-rules-inverting.explanation: G = −R_f/R_in = −4.7, so V_out = −4.7 × 0.20 = -0.94 V. The input current is 20 µA, and it all flows through R_f.

e0-l025-opamp-golden-rules-inverting.prompt: Explain, in your own words, how negative feedback gives the golden rules and why the gain depends on resistors rather than on the op-amp.
e0-l025-opamp-golden-rules-inverting.rubric: Full credit: (1) the op-amp has huge open-loop gain, so a finite output needs a nearly zero differential input; (2) feedback feeds a fraction of the output back to the inverting input so that it reduces any difference, forcing V_- ≈ V_+; (3) with V_- fixed and no input current, the gain is set by the resistor ratio (divider/current balance), not by A.
e0-l025-opamp-golden-rules-inverting.modelAnswer: The op-amp multiplies the input difference by a huge A, so with a finite output the difference must be almost zero. Negative feedback routes a fraction of the output to the inverting input so any difference is corrected, which holds V_− close to V_+. With no current entering the inputs, the signal current through R_in must pass through R_f, so the gain depends only on the resistor ratio, and A, which varies with temperature and part, cancels out.

e0-l026-opamp-noninverting-buffer.prompt: What is the purpose of a unity-gain buffer (voltage follower) between a pH electrode and a data-acquisition input?
options: It amplifies the electrode's signal tenfold, so that the small voltage can be digitised accurately
It matches the impedance of the electrode to that of the ADC, so that maximum power is transferred to the converter
It converts the electrode's current into a voltage, so that the ADC can read it directly
It gives the electrode a very high input resistance and the ADC a low source resistance, so no voltage is lost
e0-l026-opamp-noninverting-buffer.explanation: The follower has gain 1, so it does not amplify. Its value is impedance transformation: a ~100 MΩ source sees a (near) infinite input resistance and the ADC sees a low-resistance source, avoiding the divider error.

e0-l026-opamp-noninverting-buffer.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier with gain 10 is powered from ±5 V, and a 1.0 V input is applied. What does the output do?
options: It reaches 10 V, because the golden rules guarantee V_out = 10 V_in for any supply voltage you might choose to use
It clips near the +5 V rail rather than reaching 10 V, because the output cannot exceed the supply
It reaches 10 V only briefly, and then falls back to 5 V as the feedback corrects the gain
It stays at 0 V, because the input is too large for the op-amp, which switches itself off
e0-l026-opamp-noninverting-buffer.explanation: The golden rules assume the output is in its linear range. An op-amp cannot output more than (roughly) its supply voltage, so with 10 V demanded from a ±5 V supply the output clips near +5 V and V_- no longer follows V_+.

e0-l026-opamp-noninverting-buffer.prompt: An op-amp with gain–bandwidth product 2.0 MHz is used as a non-inverting amplifier with R_f = 90 kΩ and R_g = 10 kΩ. What is its approximate −3 dB bandwidth? (Give the answer in kHz.)
e0-l026-opamp-noninverting-buffer.explanation: The gain is 1 + 90/10 = 10, so the bandwidth is GBW/G = 2000 kHz/10 = 200 kHz. Trading gain for bandwidth is why a high-gain stage is often split into two lower-gain ones.

e0-l026-opamp-noninverting-buffer.prompt: Show how the non-inverting gain 1 + R_f/R_g follows from the golden rules, and say why its gain can never be less than 1.
e0-l026-opamp-noninverting-buffer.rubric: Full credit: (1) V_- = V_in by the first rule; (2) V_- is the divider output of V_out through R_f and R_g: V_- = V_out R_g/(R_f+R_g); (3) so V_out = V_in(1+R_f/R_g), which is at least 1 since R_f/R_g ≥ 0.
e0-l026-opamp-noninverting-buffer.modelAnswer: By the first golden rule the inverting input equals V_in. It is also the output of a divider across V_out made of R_f and R_g, so V_in = V_out R_g/(R_f + R_g). Rearranging gives V_out = V_in(1 + R_f/R_g). Because R_f/R_g cannot be negative, the gain is at least 1.

e0-l027-transimpedance-amplifier.prompt: In a photodiode transimpedance amplifier, why is it useful that the photodiode sits at (virtual) zero volts?
options: Zero volts across the diode makes the photocurrent largest, because the junction is then most sensitive to light
With zero bias the diode has little dark current and a linear response, and all the photocurrent flows into R_f
The diode converts light to voltage directly, and the virtual ground keeps that voltage from being loaded by R_f
Zero volts keeps the diode in forward conduction, so it behaves as a battery that is charged by the light
e0-l027-transimpedance-amplifier.explanation: The inverting input is held at about 0 V, so the diode sees no bias: dark current and its voltage dependence are minimal, and the entire photocurrent (the op-amp draws none) flows through R_f to give V_out = −I R_f.

e0-l027-transimpedance-amplifier.prompt: R_f is increased from 1 MΩ to 100 MΩ with the same feedback capacitor C_f. What is the main consequence?
options: The gain and the bandwidth both rise 100-fold, because a larger resistor gives a larger and faster signal
The gain rises 100-fold and the bandwidth stays the same, since bandwidth depends only on the op-amp used
The gain stays the same and the bandwidth falls, since only the capacitor determines the gain of the stage
The gain rises 100-fold, but the bandwidth 1/(2πR_fC_f) falls 100-fold, so the response is slower and its noise current is lower
e0-l027-transimpedance-amplifier.explanation: V_out = −I R_f scales with R_f, but the pole f_c = 1/(2πR_fC_f) moves down in proportion. Larger R_f also has lower relative Johnson-noise current (i_n ∝ 1/√R_f), so low-current measurements use large R_f and accept the slow response.

e0-l027-transimpedance-amplifier.prompt: A photodiode current of 5.0 nA must be turned into 1.0 V at the output. What feedback resistor R_f is needed? (Give the answer in MΩ.)
