e0-l027-transimpedance-amplifier.explanation: |V_out| = I R_f, so R_f = 1.0 V / 5.0×10⁻⁹ A = 2.0e+08 Ω = 200 MΩ. Such large values need low-leakage layout and a small C_f to keep the bandwidth up.

e0-l027-transimpedance-amplifier.prompt: Why is a TIA a better way to measure a small electrochemical or photocurrent than putting a series resistor in the circuit and measuring the voltage across it?
e0-l027-transimpedance-amplifier.rubric: Full credit: (1) a series resistor creates a burden voltage that changes the voltage across the cell/diode, so the measured current is disturbed and may become non-linear; (2) the TIA holds the input at virtual ground so the source sees ~0 V regardless of current; (3) the output is a low-impedance voltage proportional to current, with gain set by R_f.
e0-l027-transimpedance-amplifier.modelAnswer: A series resistor puts a voltage drop I·R in the circuit, so the electrode or photodiode no longer sees the voltage you intended and its response can become non-linear. The TIA keeps its input at virtual ground, so the source is not disturbed no matter how large the current or R_f. It also converts the current to a low-impedance voltage with a gain set by R_f.

e0-l028-adc-dac-resolution.prompt: An instrument's 12-bit ADC is replaced by a 16-bit one. When will the extra bits improve the measurement?
options: Only when analogue noise is already below the new, smaller step; otherwise the extra bits just digitise noise from the front end
Always, because every added bit halves the error of the measurement, whatever noise comes before the converter
Only when the sampling rate is also increased by a factor of 16, since resolution and speed rise together
Never, because the resolution is set by the signal source and not by the number of bits in the converter
e0-l028-adc-dac-resolution.explanation: Each bit halves the step (LSB = V_FS/2^N), but if the analogue signal carries noise larger than an LSB the extra bits resolve only noise. Resolution in practice is limited by the noise of the front end.

e0-l028-adc-dac-resolution.prompt: Why is an analogue low-pass (anti-alias) filter placed before an ADC?
options: It lowers the noise to below one LSB, which is the only requirement the converter places on its input
It converts the signal from AC to DC, which is the form that ADCs require at their input
Content above half the sampling rate folds into the band as false signals that cannot be removed later
It increases the number of bits available, since a smoother signal is quantised more finely
e0-l028-adc-dac-resolution.explanation: Sampling at f_s cannot distinguish a frequency f from f_s − f, so unfiltered content above f_s/2 appears as false peaks at lower frequency (aliasing). Only an analogue filter before the ADC can stop it.

e0-l028-adc-dac-resolution.prompt: A 16-bit ADC has a 0–10 V input range. What is the size of one least-significant bit? (Give the answer in µV.)
e0-l028-adc-dac-resolution.explanation: LSB = V_FS/2^N = 10 V/65536 = 152.6 µV. The ideal rms quantisation noise is LSB/√12 = 44.0 µV.

e0-l028-adc-dac-resolution.prompt: Describe in words how a 3-bit R-2R ladder DAC produces an output for the code 101, and what this has to do with voltage dividers.
e0-l028-adc-dac-resolution.rubric: Full credit: (1) each bit switches its branch to V_ref (1) or ground (0); (2) the ladder of R and 2R acts as a repeated voltage divider, so bit k contributes V_ref/2^k (MSB V_ref/2, next V_ref/4, LSB V_ref/8); (3) the output is the sum, 101 → V_ref(1/2 + 1/8) = 0.625 V_ref.
e0-l028-adc-dac-resolution.modelAnswer: Each bit connects its branch of the ladder either to the reference voltage or to ground. The R and 2R resistors divide the voltage so that the most significant bit contributes V_ref/2, the next V_ref/4 and the least V_ref/8, and the output is the sum of the contributions (superposition). For code 101 that is V_ref(1/2 + 1/8) = 0.625 V_ref, i.e. 5/8 of full scale.

e0-l029-noise-averaging-lockin.prompt: Why does averaging N repeated scans improve the signal-to-noise ratio by √N and not by N?
options: Only the square root of the scans are usable, since the others are used up in removing the baseline
The signal and the noise both grow as N, but the instrument adds a fixed noise that increases as √N
Noise cancels exactly between successive scans, so the leftover noise is the square root of the number of scans
The signal adds directly (grows as N), while random noise adds in quadrature (grows as √N)
e0-l029-noise-averaging-lockin.explanation: The signal is the same in each scan, so N scans sum to N×. Independent random noise adds as variance, so its rms grows only as √N. SNR improves by N/√N = √N: this is why an NMR experiment needs four times as many scans for twice the SNR.

e0-l029-noise-averaging-lockin.prompt: What does a lock-in amplifier (or modulating the signal) do to improve a measurement?
options: It amplifies the whole spectrum equally, so that the signal and the noise are both raised above the ADC's quantisation noise
It moves the signal to a chosen frequency and measures only a very narrow band around it, away from 1/f noise and mains hum
It averages the signal over a long time, which removes any noise at the frequency of the signal as well as other frequencies
It subtracts a recorded copy of the noise, which works for any noise source, random or not
e0-l029-noise-averaging-lockin.explanation: Noise power grows with bandwidth, so a very narrow detection band (set by the lock-in's time constant) rejects almost all of it. Modulation (a chopped beam, AC excitation) puts the signal at a frequency where the noise floor is low.

e0-l029-noise-averaging-lockin.prompt: What is the rms Johnson noise voltage of a 1.0 MΩ resistor at 300 K measured in a 10 kHz bandwidth? (Use v_n = √(4k_BTRΔf); give the answer in µV.)
e0-l029-noise-averaging-lockin.explanation: v_n = √(4 × 1.381×10⁻²³ × 300 × 10⁶ × 10⁴) = 12.9 µV. A 1 MΩ sensor therefore cannot resolve signals much below ~10 µV in that bandwidth, unless the bandwidth is narrowed.

e0-l029-noise-averaging-lockin.prompt: An NMR spectrum recorded with 16 scans has SNR = 10, and you want SNR = 40. Roughly how many scans do you need, and why?
e0-l029-noise-averaging-lockin.rubric: Full credit: (1) SNR ∝ √N, so a factor of 4 in SNR needs 4² = 16 times as many scans, i.e. about 256; (2) because signal adds as N and random noise as √N; (3) optionally comments on cost in time (16× the acquisition time).
e0-l029-noise-averaging-lockin.modelAnswer: SNR grows as the square root of the number of scans, so a fourfold gain needs 16 times as many scans: 16 × 16 = 256 scans. The signal adds up linearly with the number of scans while the random noise adds in quadrature, so the experiment takes 16 times longer for a fourfold gain in SNR.

e0-l030-potentiostat-block-diagram.prompt: What is the role of the reference electrode in a three-electrode potentiostat?
options: It carries the full cell current back to the instrument, so that all of the charge is accounted for in the measurement
It acts as a second working electrode and doubles the current signal measured by the transimpedance stage
It provides a stable potential reference and is sensed at very high impedance, so almost no current flows through it
It supplies the programmed voltage waveform to the cell, so that the control amplifier needs no counter electrode
e0-l030-potentiostat-block-diagram.explanation: Because the reference is read by a high-impedance input it carries negligible current, so its potential stays fixed (no polarisation, little iR error). The control amplifier adjusts the counter electrode until the measured working–reference potential equals the programmed value.

e0-l030-potentiostat-block-diagram.prompt: Why does a potentiostat use a separate counter electrode instead of passing the cell current through the reference electrode?
options: The counter electrode carries the current, so the reference stays unpolarised with a stable, well-defined potential
The counter electrode has the lower resistance, so the measurement can be made with a smaller supply voltage
The reference electrode is too large, so the current would spread through it and distort the measured voltammogram
Current in the reference electrode would be measured twice, once at the working electrode and once at the reference
e0-l030-potentiostat-block-diagram.explanation: If current passed through the reference electrode its potential would drift (polarisation, iR drop), defeating its purpose. The counter electrode can swing to whatever potential is needed to push the current; its voltage is limited by the compliance voltage.

e0-l030-potentiostat-block-diagram.prompt: In a cyclic-voltammetry cell, 50 µA flows through a solution with 500 Ω of uncompensated resistance between the reference tip and the working electrode. By how much does the true electrode potential differ from the applied one? (Give the answer in mV.)
e0-l030-potentiostat-block-diagram.explanation: ΔE = iR_u = 50×10⁻⁶ A × 500 Ω = 25 mV. This is why peaks shift and broaden at high currents, and why potentiostats offer iR compensation.

e0-l030-potentiostat-block-diagram.prompt: Follow a cyclic-voltammetry experiment through the potentiostat blocks: which block produces the triangular waveform, which keeps the potential at the programmed value, and how does the measured current become a number in a file?
e0-l030-potentiostat-block-diagram.rubric: Full credit: (1) a DAC (or waveform generator) makes the programmed triangle; (2) the control amplifier compares reference vs programmed potential and drives the counter electrode to make them equal; (3) the working-electrode current goes into a transimpedance (current-to-voltage) stage with V = -I R_f, then through an ADC to a digital value.
e0-l030-potentiostat-block-diagram.modelAnswer: A DAC (or function generator) produces the triangular potential programme. The control amplifier compares the reference electrode's potential with it and drives the counter electrode until they agree. The current at the working electrode, held at virtual ground, goes into a transimpedance amplifier that gives V = −I R_f, and an ADC samples that voltage and the potential so that the computer records the voltammogram as pairs of numbers.

e0-l031-detector-signal-chains.prompt: Why does the first amplifier stage mostly set the noise of a receiver chain such as an NMR spectrometer's?
options: The first stage carries the largest signal, and noise is always proportional to the size of the signal
Noise added by later stages is amplified by the first stage's gain, making them the largest contributors
Later stages' noise is divided by the gain before them, so a low-noise, high-gain first stage dominates
The first stage is the only one that adds noise, since later stages operate on a signal that is already clean
e0-l031-detector-signal-chains.explanation: In the cascade formula F = F₁ + (F₂−1)/G₁ + …, later stages are divided by the gain in front of them. A low-noise preamplifier with high gain at the probe therefore sets the whole system's sensitivity.

e0-l031-detector-signal-chains.prompt: An electron-multiplier ion detector in a mass spectrometer switches from pulse-counting to analogue mode at very high ion rates. Why?
options: At high rates pulses overlap and are missed (dead time), so counting saturates while the analogue current stays linear
Counting works only at high rates, and the analogue mode is used at low rates because it has no noise
At high rates each ion produces a much smaller pulse, so the discriminator no longer detects it as a count
Analogue mode is always more precise, and counting is used only when an instrument has no TIA available
e0-l031-detector-signal-chains.explanation: Each ion produces a pulse of finite width, so at high rates pulses merge and counts are lost. The average current (a TIA output) stays linear. At low rates, counting individual pulses rejects amplifier noise and gives the best sensitivity.

e0-l031-detector-signal-chains.prompt: A receiver has a preamplifier with noise factor F₁ = 1.26 (1 dB) and gain G₁ = 100 (20 dB), followed by a second stage with F₂ = 10. What is the total noise factor of the chain? (Use F = F₁ + (F₂−1)/G₁; give a number.)
e0-l031-detector-signal-chains.explanation: F = 1.26 + (10 − 1)/100 = 1.35, about 1.30 dB. The poor second stage adds only 0.3 dB because the preamplifier's gain hides it.

e0-l031-detector-signal-chains.prompt: Trace an NMR signal from the sample to the digital spectrum, naming the role of each stage in the receiver chain and the circuit idea from earlier lessons that it uses.
e0-l031-detector-signal-chains.rubric: Full credit: (1) tuned and matched LC coil (resonance, Q) picks up the µV FID at the Larmor frequency; (2) low-noise preamplifier (noise figure, first stage dominates); (3) mixer with local oscillator shifts to a low frequency (difference frequency), then low-pass/anti-alias filter (RC filter), (4) ADC samples and digitises (resolution, Nyquist); FFT then makes the spectrum.
e0-l031-detector-signal-chains.modelAnswer: The sample's precessing magnetisation induces a microvolt signal in the probe coil, which is a tuned, matched LC circuit at the Larmor frequency. A low-noise preamplifier boosts it, because the first stage sets the noise. A mixer multiplies by a local oscillator to shift the signal down to a difference frequency in the kHz range, a low-pass anti-alias filter limits the bandwidth, and the ADC samples it. The digital FID is then Fourier-transformed into the spectrum.
